ai.definition: Blockchain for Voting Systems is a technology that leverages blockchain's decentralized ledger capabilities to enhance the security, transparency, and integrity of electoral processes.
ai.howItWorks: By implementing a distributed network where each participant has a copy of the transaction history, blockchain ensures that once data (votes) are recorded, they cannot be altered or deleted without consensus from the majority of participants. This is achieved through cryptographic hashes, which link blocks in the chain and create an immutable record.
ai.problemSolved: Fraudulent activities such as double voting, vote tampering, and electoral manipulation can be significantly reduced by using blockchain technology.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves developing smart contracts to automate certain aspects of the voting process, coding these into a blockchain platform, and integrating with existing voter databases or identity verification systems.
ai.buildProcess: Developing a blockchain-based voting system requires extensive testing in simulated environments, followed by rigorous security audits. Pilot tests are often conducted before full-scale deployment to ensure reliability and address any unforeseen issues.
ai.costDrivers: High costs associated with robust cybersecurity measures, legal compliance, and ensuring user privacy. Additionally, the need for advanced hardware and software development can significantly increase expenses.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: While still in the early stages of widespread adoption, blockchain-based voting systems are expected to gain traction as trust in electoral processes becomes increasingly important.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for blockchain technology and its application in governance are still evolving. Countries may have different laws regarding data privacy, security standards, and the use of blockchain in public services.
ai.risks: Technical risks include potential vulnerabilities in smart contract code, scalability issues with large-scale voting systems, and the challenge of ensuring user anonymity while maintaining transparency. Political risks involve resistance from traditional governance structures and concerns over centralization efforts.
ai.profitability: The profitability of blockchain-based voting systems is not immediately apparent as they are often government-funded projects aimed at improving democratic processes rather than generating revenue.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development may focus on enhancing user experience, expanding the scope to include more types of elections and referendums, and integrating with other technologies like AI for better data analysis.

glossary.def: A decentralized digital ledger that records transactions across multiple computers in a secure and tamper-proof way.
A self-executing contract with the terms of the agreement directly written into code.

subsystems.name: Eligibility and enrolment
subsystems.role: decides who is allowed to vote and issues each voter a one-time credential.

subsystems.name: Ballot client
subsystems.role: the device software that presents the ballot and encrypts the choice before anything leaves the voter's hands.

subsystems.name: Cryptographic protocol
subsystems.role: lets votes be counted without revealing individual choices.

subsystems.name: Distributed ledger
subsystems.role: an append-only, tamper-evident record of cast ballots, replicated across independent organisations.

subsystems.name: Public bulletin board
subsystems.role: a place where voters and observers can check that their ballot was recorded and included in the tally.

subsystems.name: Tally and audit
subsystems.role: turns the sealed record into a published result with proofs.

subsystems.name: Key management
subsystems.role: protects the keys that decrypt the result; whoever holds them could break secrecy.

buildSteps.title: Fix the trust model
buildSteps.detail: Decide who runs the nodes, who holds decryption keys and what the system must survive — a corrupt official, a hacked phone, or a lying vendor.

buildSteps.title: Build the electoral roll and credentials
buildSteps.detail: Link each eligible voter to a single-use credential without storing the link between identity and vote on the ledger.

buildSteps.title: Build the ballot client
buildSteps.detail: Write software that encrypts the vote on the voter's own device and produces a receipt the voter can later check, and harden it against malware and screen capture.

buildSteps.title: Design the counting cryptography
buildSteps.detail: Choose either homomorphic encryption, where encrypted votes are added without decrypting them, or a mix-net that shuffles and re-encrypts ballots; add proofs that every recorded ballot is well-formed.

buildSteps.title: Deploy the ledger
buildSteps.detail: Stand up validator nodes at separate organisations, such as electoral commissions, parties and auditors, and write each cast ballot as a transaction with the voter's proof of eligibility.

buildSteps.title: Publish a verifiable record
buildSteps.detail: Publish the ballot set, or a hash of it, so anyone can independently verify that the tally matches the recorded votes.

buildSteps.title: Tally and prove
buildSteps.detail: Combine or decrypt the sealed votes under threshold keys, publish the proofs, and run audits that detect any mismatch.

buildSteps.title: Operate and rehearse
buildSteps.detail: Run key ceremonies, penetration tests and full failed-election rehearsals, because a voting system must degrade to a paper fallback, not to no result.

prerequisites.why: mix-nets, homomorphic tallying and zero-knowledge proofs exist and have been used in small elections, but not at national scale.
the ledger is only as trustworthy as the enrolment step that stops one person voting twice.
a phone or home computer can silently alter a vote before it is encrypted, and no ledger can detect this.
remote voting from home cannot prevent a vote being bought or cast under pressure, which is why polling booths exist.
election-night volumes and simultaneous national access stress systems that are proven mainly in small pilots.
statistical audits of paper ballots catch errors that a purely digital record cannot.

pathway.milestone: blockchain-anchored records alongside paper voting, plus pilots for low-risk groups such as overseas or military voters and corporate proxy voting
pathway.unlocks: tamper-evident audit trails and real-world test data without risking a general election.

pathway.milestone: end-to-end verifiable internet voting with in-person enrolment and single-use credentials, used in binding municipal or organisational elections
pathway.unlocks: voters can check their own ballot was counted, while paper remains the legal record.

pathway.milestone: coercion-resistant remote voting designs tested in real elections
pathway.unlocks: remote voting that does not create new ways to pressure voters.

pathway.milestone: national general elections counted partly on distributed ledgers with independent node operators
pathway.unlocks: transparent, observer-verifiable tallies — but only if device security, identity and privacy problems are solved first, and blockchain by itself solves none of them.
